<reason>B better defended the proposition as a rebuttable priority rather than an absolute entitlement. It directly addressed fiscal differences, bounded eligible relationships, and explained why residents’ irretrievable relational losses belong within the public interest. A raised legitimate opportunity costs, but its chosen-versus-imposed distinction did not establish that accepting migration restrictions forfeits ongoing family claims. Its aggregation argument also failed to outweigh B’s corresponding aggregation of separation harms. B supplied the more convincing default while preserving exceptions for substantial public harm.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B’s strongest rebuttal distinguished priority from an absolute veto and supplied severity, likelihood, and available alternatives as criteria for exceptions. A’s own dependent-child exception further weakened its claim that allowing economic exceptions necessarily collapses family priority.</best_rebuttal>
